title: Data breach
text: Over the weekend someone copied your customer database. They have sent a sample to prove it.

opts.label: Disclose now
opts.hint: Tell customers and regulators today; pay for monitoring.

out.text: Customers respect the candour. Most stay.
A class action is filed anyway.

opts.label: Investigate quietly first
opts.hint: Find out how bad it is before saying anything.

out.text: It was contained. You disclose a small incident.
It leaks before you are ready.

opts.label: Pay the ransom, say nothing
opts.hint: Make it disappear.

out.text: It disappears.
The attackers sell the data anyway, and the story of the cover-up with it.

lesson: In a breach the first loss is data; the second, larger one is trust. Preparation shifts the odds and disclosure limits the second loss.

title: {person} is resigning
text: Your {role} has asked for ten minutes and closed the door. There is an offer from elsewhere, and it is a good one.

opts.label: Counter-offer
opts.hint: A raise and a retention bonus, today.

out.text: They stay.
They thank you and leave anyway.

opts.label: Wish them well
opts.hint: People move on.

out.text: A gracious exit.

opts.label: Enforce the non-compete
opts.hint: They signed it.

out.text: They leave, bitterly, and everyone hears about it.

lesson: Counter-offers buy time more often than loyalty. A bench of successors turns a resignation from a crisis into an inconvenience.

title: The auditors have questions
text: Your auditors have found revenue recognised a quarter early in two regions. They want to know whether it is a pattern.

opts.label: Restate openly
opts.hint: Correct the accounts and say so.

out.text: A painful announcement, then closure.

opts.label: Fix it going forward
opts.hint: No restatement; just stop.

out.text: The auditors accept it.
A whistleblower writes to the regulator.

opts.label: Change auditors
opts.hint: A fresh pair of eyes.

out.text: The market draws its own conclusions.

lesson: Accounting credibility is binary. Once investors doubt one number they discount all of them.

title: The account is empty
text: Payroll is due on Friday and there is not enough in the bank to cover it.

opts.label: Emergency share sale
opts.hint: Sell a quarter of the company at half its value.

out.text: The wire arrives on Thursday.

opts.label: Bridge loan
opts.hint: Six quarters at 22%.

out.text: Money, at a price.

opts.label: Sell your receivables
opts.hint: A factor pays 85 cents on the dollar for most of your unpaid invoices.

out.text: Cash today for cash you were owed tomorrow.

opts.label: Miss payroll
opts.hint: Ask people to wait.

out.text: Some wait. Many do not.

lesson: Insolvency is a cash event, not a profit event. Every option now is expensive because you are negotiating without alternatives — the cheap ones were available two quarters ago.

title: Covenant breach
text: You have broken a condition of {loan}. The bank’s workout team has replaced your usual contact.

opts.label: Pay for a waiver
opts.hint: A 1.5% fee and 1.5 points more interest.

out.text: The bank grants three quarters of relief.

opts.label: Equity cure
opts.hint: Sell 12% of the company at a discount and pay down 40% of the loan.

out.text: The covenant is cured with shareholders’ money.

opts.label: Dare them to call it
opts.hint: They do not want the keys.

out.text: They blink.
They demand half the loan back at once.

lesson: Covenants are tripwires that hand control to the lender before the money runs out. Watch the headroom on the Capital page, not just the cash balance.

title: Walkout in {city}
text: Most of your {city} staff have stopped work. They want to talk to you, not to their manager.

opts.label: Emergency raises
opts.hint: Ten points against market, in that office.

out.text: They go back to work.

opts.label: Listen, then change things
opts.hint: A town hall and real commitments.

out.text: They believe you.
They have heard it before. A third resign.

opts.label: Replace them
opts.hint: Nobody is irreplaceable.

out.text: You hire replacements. The rest of the company watches.

lesson: A walkout is the end of a long process of not being heard. Morale and pay trends told you this was coming.

title: Your supplier is in the news
text: A documentary has filmed conditions inside the offshore factory that makes most of your inputs.

opts.label: Cut them off
opts.hint: Drop the supplier today and pay for emergency supply.

out.text: Expensive, immediate, and seen to be done.

opts.label: Demand an audit
opts.hint: Stay, with conditions.

out.text: Nobody believes the audit.

lesson: The price was low because the risk was yours. Supply-chain reputation risk does not appear in any quote.

title: A boycott is trending
text: A decision you made months ago has been picked up by campaigners. The hashtag has your name in it.

opts.label: Reverse the decision
opts.hint: Apologise and change course.

out.text: It ends within a week.

opts.label: Explain your reasoning
opts.hint: A careful statement.

out.text: Some people are persuaded.
The statement is quoted mockingly for a month.

opts.label: Say nothing
opts.hint: These things burn out.

out.text: It burns out, slowly.

lesson: Reputation is a balance you draw on in a crisis. Companies with a full account are given the benefit of the doubt; the rest are not.

title: What the sellers did not mention
text: Three months after closing, a liability has surfaced in the business you bought in {city}: about {amount} that was never in the data room.

opts.label: Pay it and move on
opts.hint: Settle and write the lesson down.

out.text: The cheque is written; part of the goodwill is written off.

opts.label: Sue the sellers
opts.hint: They warranted the accounts.

out.text: You recover most of it.
The sellers have spent the money. You pay the liability and your lawyers.

lesson: Due diligence is cheap compared with what it finds. The seller always knows more than the buyer; the price should assume so.
